title: Decomposition Rules: How Orchestrators Break Down Work for Subagents
body:
Work decomposition determines output quality and coordination overhead. Poor decomposition causes voice inconsistency, scope overlap, wasted work, handoff failures, and merge collisions. Decomposition happens before execution, not during it.

**Core Decomposition Principles:**

**Decompose by Function, Not by Chunk Size.** Wrong: split a 3,000-word document into three 1,000-word chunks. Right: split into discrete functional stages — discovery, briefing, outlining, per-section drafting, merge normalization, QA — with per-section drafters running in parallel within the drafting stage. Chunk-based decomposition produces voice inconsistency at chunk boundaries, repeated content at seams, and structural incoherence.

**Assign Bounded Scopes.** Each subagent must have one clear scope that it owns completely. Scopes must not overlap. A scope definition must specify: what the agent is responsible for producing; what inputs it receives and from which prior stage; what outputs it produces (format and schema); what it is explicitly not responsible for. If you cannot write a clear scope definition, the decomposition is not ready.

**Separate Writing from Reviewing.** A subagent that drafts a section must not also review it. Route all finished drafts through a distinct review agent. This applies even in single-agent workflows: complete the draft, then switch to review mode explicitly.

**Normalize at Merge Time, Not Drafting Time.** Multiple subagents writing parallel sections will produce inconsistent voice and tone — this is expected. Do not try to enforce voice consistency during parallel drafting. Instead: run a dedicated merge-normalizer agent after assembly. The merge-normalizer's only job is voice and style consistency; it does not revise content, structure, or accuracy.

**Define Handoff Formats Before Dispatching.** Every agent handoff must use a defined schema or structured format. Valid handoff formats include: JSON conforming to a named schema, structured markdown with defined required sections, checklists with pass/fail fields, issue lists with classification fields. If a receiving agent cannot parse the handoff without reading prose for context, the handoff format is invalid.

**Scope Maximum Rule.** No single subagent should own more than: one document section (for section-drafter agents); one review perspective (for qa-* agents); one workflow stage (for orchestration-layer agents).

**Standard Document Decomposition Sequence:** (1) discovery-agent — sequential, must complete before brief; (2) brief-writer — sequential, must complete before outline; (3) outline-architect — sequential, must complete before section drafting; (4) section-drafter x N — parallel, all run concurrently; (5) merge-normalizer — sequential, after all section drafts complete; (6) qa-* agents — parallel, all run concurrently on the same document; (7) lead-editor — sequential, final gate.

**Parallelization Rules:** Safe to parallelize: section drafters, QA agents, guide creation agents. Must be sequential: discovery → brief → outline → [parallel drafting] → merge → [parallel QA] → final; any step where output of step N is input of step N+1; any step that writes to shared state.

**Anti-Patterns:** One-agent-does-everything; chunk-based splits; skipping merge-normalization; vague handoffs; overlapping QA scopes; skipping discovery.
